fields.foundation: The Srivijaya Empire was the dominant maritime power of Southeast Asia from the seventh to the thirteenth centuries. It was a thalassocracy, built on control of the sea lanes and on revenue taken from the traffic passing through the Strait of Malacca and the waters around Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, not on territorial conquest and agricultural surplus. Its origins are obscure. The first clear description comes from the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Yijing (I-Tsing), who stopped there in 671 CE on his way to study in India and described a thriving centre of Buddhist learning with more than a thousand monks, comparable to the great monasteries of India; Chinese sources record the polity as Shilifoshi. The Kedukan Bukit inscription of 682 CE, found near modern Palembang and written in Old Malay, among the earliest surviving examples of that language, records the ruler Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa leading a military expedition and establishing his authority over the surrounding region. Palembang on the Musi River in southern Sumatra was the empire's core capital, placed to control shipping moving between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea through the Malacca and Sunda straits. The empire did not arise from a single act of conquest. It formed gradually from a network of Malay chieftaincies that the rulers of Palembang brought under tributary suzerainty through military pressure, commercial incentive and the deliberate use of Buddhist religious legitimacy. The Sailendra dynasty, which appears to have been closely connected to Srivijaya from the eighth century, built the great Buddhist monument of Borobudur in central Java, which suggests that Srivijayan cultural and political influence reached across the Java Sea at the empire's height.
fields.socioeconomy: The Srivijayan economy was a transit economy: the empire prospered by taxing the movement of goods through the maritime corridors it controlled, not by producing them. The Strait of Malacca was the principal bottleneck for seaborne trade between China and the Indian subcontinent, and Srivijaya's control of the ports and anchorages on both sides of it allowed the empire to levy harbour fees, customs duties and protection payments on merchants of every nationality. Chinese ceramics and silk, Indian textiles and spices, and luxury goods from the Persian Gulf and Arabia all moved through Srivijayan waters. The revenues were enough to support a substantial fleet, a Buddhist monastic establishment of international repute, and a court that exchanged regular embassies with Tang and later Song China. The polity itself produced relatively little for export: Sumatra's interior yielded forest products, including camphor, benzoin resin and aromatic woods, as well as alluvial gold, which supplemented commercial revenues. The empire enforced its commercial dominance through naval force and through oaths of loyalty (sumpah), preserved in inscriptions such as those of Kota Kapur and Telaga Batu, whose elaborate curse formulae bound subordinate port polities and officials to Palembang. Merchant communities from China, India, Arabia and the wider Malay world kept permanent quarters in the major ports, which made them cosmopolitan commercial centres. The empire's prosperity was therefore tied directly to the volume of trade passing through the region. That dependence left it vulnerable to shifting trade routes, the rise of competing ports and the appearance of naval powers able to challenge its supremacy at sea.
fields.military: The Srivijayan military was primarily a naval force, organised around the war fleets whose control of the Malacca Strait supported the empire's whole economic and political system. Much of its strength came from the orang laut, the 'sea people', maritime communities who had lived on their boats among the islands of Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula for generations. Their seamanship, local knowledge and capacity for rapid mobilisation made them the most effective maritime force in the region. The orang laut were not soldiers in the conventional sense but a client population whose loyalty Srivijaya secured through patronage, and their naval service was the empire's main means of coercion. Srivijaya could also project power over considerable distances. When the Javanese kingdom of Medang under Dharmawangsa attacked Sumatra around 990 CE, Srivijaya withstood the assault, and in 1016 the Medang court was destroyed by a rebellion of the vassal ruler of Wurawari, an event many historians attribute to Srivijayan backing or regard as a Srivijayan invasion of Medang. The most serious challenge came from South India. In 1025 the Chola king Rajendra Chola I launched a great naval raid that sacked Srivijaya and a string of its ports, including Kadaram (Kedah) and Malaiyur, and captured its ruler Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman; a further Chola expedition followed around 1068 under Virarajendra. These raids exposed a structural weakness: faced with a power willing to send a concentrated fleet from outside the region, Srivijaya's dispersed network of orang laut auxiliaries could not mount a sustained defence. They did not destroy its commercial position outright, but they showed the limits of its military capacity and allowed rival ports to assert greater independence.
fields.governance: Scholars have described Srivijaya's government as a 'galactic polity' or mandala: a centre-periphery arrangement in which the paramount ruler at Palembang exercised suzerainty over subordinate port lords who kept substantial autonomy within a framework of ritual submission, commercial obligation and periodic tribute. The empire's authority rested more on commercial incentives and religious prestige than on the direct administration and territorial garrisons characteristic of continental Asian empires. Subordinate rulers were bound to the paramount through oath-taking ceremonies backed by Buddhist ritual and the threat of supernatural punishment. For most of them the prospect of commercial exclusion, denial of access to Srivijayan-controlled trade networks, was a more effective sanction than military force. The ruler's legitimacy was framed within Mahayana and later Vajrayana Buddhism, and he was probably presented as a figure of great spiritual merit, possibly a bodhisattva, whose authority derived from accumulated virtue. The promotion of Srivijaya as a major centre of Buddhist learning, which Yijing recommended to Chinese monks as a place to study before travelling on to India, served several purposes at once: it attracted pilgrims and their patronage, reinforced the ruler's religious standing, and created a network of monastic foundations that carried Srivijayan influence beyond the reach of its fleets. Srivijayan rulers also endowed Buddhist foundations abroad, including a monastery at Nalanda in Bihar and the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam on the Chola coast. Administrative records are sparse, as would be expected of a commercial thalassocracy with a modest bureaucracy compared with that of a territorial agrarian empire.
fields.impact: Srivijaya was the founding commercial and cultural intermediary of maritime Southeast Asia, and the trade networks, commercial practices and religious culture it established influenced the later development of the whole region. For some six centuries it was the principal node linking the commercial systems of China, India, the Islamic world and the islands of Southeast Asia, and it made the Strait of Malacca one of the most commercially important maritime passages in Asia. Its patronage of Mahayana Buddhism encouraged a synthesis of Indian and local traditions that shaped the art, architecture and religious practice of the region; the temple complexes of Muaro Jambi and Muara Takus in Sumatra, and the Sailendra monuments of central Java, rank among the finest achievements of Asian religious art. Old Malay, used in Srivijaya's inscriptions and spread as a language of commerce across its network, was an ancestor of the Malay language that later became one of the most widely spoken languages of Southeast Asia. The commercial infrastructure Srivijaya developed, with dependable harbour facilities, predictable customs procedures and the protection of merchant shipping, set the pattern for the entrepôt system later followed by Malacca, Johor, Penang and finally Singapore. The maritime routes of the so-called Silk Road, which grew in importance as overland routes through Central Asia became less secure in the late first millennium, ran through the Srivijayan network, so that the empire was a necessary link in the long-distance commerce of the medieval Old World.
fields.decline: Srivijaya's decline was gradual and had many causes: external military pressure, the growth of competing commercial centres and a long-term shift of regional power from maritime Sumatra to agrarian Java. The Chola raids of 1025 and around 1068 did not destroy Srivijaya's commercial position, but they weakened its naval supremacy and encouraged subordinate ports to assert their independence from Palembang; by the late eleventh century the centre of power appears to have shifted to Jambi, the old Malayu. The rise of the Javanese kingdoms of Kediri, then Singhasari and Majapahit, created a powerful rival centre that contested Srivijayan cultural and commercial influence. Chinese merchants of the Song period increasingly sailed directly to the ports of South and Southeast Asia in their own ships, and so depended less on Srivijayan intermediaries. The spread of Islam through the Indian Ocean trading world brought Muslim merchants into growing prominence, and the gradual conversion of port communities in northern Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula from the late thirteenth century onwards eroded the Buddhist framework on which Srivijayan legitimacy rested. Former dependencies broke away, and in 1275 Kertanagara of Singhasari launched the Pamalayu expedition against Malayu, which further weakened the Sumatran centre. By the time Kublai Khan's envoys were seeking tribute in the region in the late thirteenth century, Srivijaya had lost most of its former power. By the fourteenth century it had effectively dissolved into the regional system from which it had emerged, and Temasek (Singapore) and later Malacca inherited its commercial role.
fields.summary: Srivijaya built the maritime commercial system and the Malay cultural framework that made the Strait of Malacca one of the world's most commercially important waterways, as it remains to the present day.
fields.teaser: Srivijaya was the dominant maritime power of Southeast Asia from the 7th to 13th centuries, controlling the Strait of Malacca and the sea trade between India and China. It was also a well-known centre of Buddhist learning.
fields.t0: Based at Palembang in Sumatra, Srivijaya was a sea power that ruled the Strait of Malacca from the 7th to the 13th century.
fields.t1: It grew rich by taxing China-India shipping and became a well-known centre of Buddhist learning, spreading Old Malay across the region.
fields.t2: Chola raids, Javanese rivals, direct Chinese shipping and the spread of Islam wore it down until Temasek and Malacca took its role.
fields.dyk: The Chinese pilgrim Yijing, who stopped there in 671, found over a thousand Buddhist monks and advised Chinese monks to study in Srivijaya before going to India.
